Minority governments are not things that worry me, in fact I am sincerely hoping for one. Ideally, as I have said previously, it will be a slim NDP minority informally propped up by the LPC so that actual discussion and consensus building between parties will be required before any legislation is passed. A process that by its nature will require discussion and consensus with the CPC as they continue to hold a significant voting block in the Senate that takes its marching orders directly from their party leader.

I am also interested in seeing how Thomas Mulcair would work with a Senate where, should he honour his promise not to appoint any, there is no NDP presence. There are currently 22 vacant seats in the Senate representing votes that would certainly assist with the passage of NDP legislation - could he resist the temptation? How would that all play with the LPC propping up an NDP minority government given Trudeaus promises with respect to appointing Senators?

These may seem tasks of monumental difficulty fraught with many and various political perils to which I say "good!!", legislation should be difficult to pass. So difficult that only the most worthwhile and necessary of legislation is worth the effort it would take to shepherd it through that arduous process..... and really, which would you prefer. That scenario or a majority government situation where the majority party leader fronts legislation and it's passage through the twin shams of debate and vote in the House and the Senate lead to the foregone conclusion of Royal Assent?

A part of me (as I have also indicated previously) thinks that a slim CPC minority that falls at the Speech from the Throne, after Trudeau and Mulcair make good on their promises not to support another Harper Government, would be interesting. The GG going to the other parties and asking who can gain and hold the confidence of The House would make for an interesting process and discussion - not to mention the equally interesting wailing and gnashing of teeth in certain political quadrants.

Ah, what interesting political times we may be entering.
